第1-2题: A community library in the Northfield district of Riverside City has extended its opening hours until ten in the evening, and has turned a former storage room on the second floor into a night study area. The change took effect at the start of this month. Library staff say the number of visitors after eight in the evening has nearly doubled since then, and most of them are students preparing for examinations. The night area has forty desks, reading lamps and a small kitchen where visitors can make tea. It is open to anyone with a library card, but seats must be booked online, and each booking is limited to three hours a day. The library says the new hours will be reviewed after six months, and if demand stays high the same arrangement may be introduced at two other branches.
第3-4题: Three students at Northfield University have designed a food packaging material that breaks down in soil within eight weeks. The material is made mainly from the fibres of grain stalks left over after harvest, mixed with a small amount of plant-based glue. In tests, the team wrapped sandwiches and fresh fruit in the material and kept them at room temperature. The packaging held its shape for four days and began to soften only after moisture reached the inner layer. Their supervisor says the hardest part was not making the material strong, but making it cheap enough to compete with ordinary plastic film. A local bakery has agreed to trial the packaging for three months from March. The team has also applied for a grant to buy a machine that can produce the material in larger sheets.
第5-7题: Riverside City will hold its annual marathon on Sunday, the twelfth of April, and the city traffic office has announced a series of road closures. From five in the morning until four in the afternoon, vehicles will not be allowed on the riverside road between the old bridge and the north gate. Six bus routes will be shortened and three will run on temporary routes through the eastern districts. The organisers expect about eighteen thousand runners, and the race will start at seven thirty. Residents who live inside the closed area will be given passes for their cars, but the passes must be collected from the community office before Friday. Ambulance and fire services will keep one lane open at all times. The traffic office advises drivers to use the ring road and to allow an extra thirty minutes for journeys on Sunday.
第8-11题: W: Professor Hale, do you have a minute? I am Mia Chen, from the second-year literature group. M: Of course, Mia. Sit down. Is this about the essay you handed in last week? W: No, actually, the essay is fine, I think. It is about next term. I am trying to work out my course plan, and I keep going round in circles.

M: Right. Let us have a look. How many credits have you completed so far? W: Sixty-two. I need a hundred and twenty to graduate, so fifty-eight to go, and three terms left. M: That is comfortable, but do not leave too much to the final term. What were you thinking of taking?

W: I wanted the advanced writing course, but it clashes with the statistics class I need for my major. M: Then take statistics first. The writing course runs every term; statistics does not. It is offered in the autumn only. W: Oh, I did not know that. So statistics this term, writing next autumn.

M: Exactly. And that leaves you a free slot. Have you considered the introduction to linguistics? W: I have, but it is four credits and I have heard the reading is heavy. M: It is heavy, but it is also the prerequisite for two courses you may want later.

M: If you are worried about the workload, take it as an extra course and drop it in the second week. There is no penalty for that. W: That is reassuring. And what about the community project, the one where students teach in local schools? M: Two credits, and it is pass or fail, so it will not touch your average. It is popular, though. Applications close at the end of this month.
W: Then I will apply tonight. Thank you, Professor. I feel much clearer now.
第12-15题: M: So, did you hear back from the landlord about the flat on Mill Street? W: I did. He says we can move in on the first of September, but the rent has gone up. It is now four hundred and eighty a month, not four hundred and fifty. M: For the whole flat, or each? W: The whole flat. So two hundred and forty each, plus bills. Honestly, that is still cheaper than the hall.

M: True. But we need to be clear about the boring stuff before we sign anything. Who does what? W: I was thinking we split it down the middle. You cook, I clean. M: That sounds fair in theory, but I know how it will go. I will cook every night, and you will clean once a week and then say you are tired.

W: That is not... okay, that is slightly fair. What do you suggest? M: Let us write a list. Cooking on weekdays, cooking at weekends, dishes, bathroom, floors and the shopping. Six jobs. We take three each, and we swap every month, so nobody is stuck with the bathroom forever.

W: I like the swap idea. Can I have the shopping? I actually enjoy it. M: Fine, but that means you also take the floors. And we need a rule for guests. W: No guests after eleven on weeknights. And whoever invites them does the extra cleaning.
M: Deal. I will write it up and send it to you tonight, and we can both sign it before we pay the deposit. W: Good. And let us keep the list on the fridge, so we cannot pretend we forgot.
第16-18题: Most people prepare for an interview by reading about the company. That is useful, but it is only half the work. The other half is preparing the evidence you will need to support your answers, and that takes longer than most candidates expect.

Start with three or four stories from your own experience: a project you finished, a problem you solved, a time you worked with difficult people. For each story, write down the situation, what you decided to do, and what happened in the end. Interviewers rarely remember a claim such as I am good with teams. They do remember a specific account of how you handled a disagreement, because it tells them what you would do next time.

Then practise saying those stories out loud. Reading them silently creates a false sense of readiness: the words feel familiar, but your mouth has never said them. Ten minutes of speaking to an empty room is worth an hour of reading. If you can, record yourself once and listen for the parts where you slow down or start again. Those are usually the places where your story is still unclear.

Finally, prepare two questions to ask at the end. Not about salary, and not about anything you could have found on the website. Ask what the team found difficult last year, or how success in the first six months would be judged. The questions you ask say as much about you as the answers you give.
第19-21题: When people say they feel tired all day, they usually blame the amount of sleep they got. Researchers who study sleep habits point out that the timing matters just as much as the length. Going to bed at midnight on Monday and at three in the morning on Saturday gives you two very different nights, and the body treats them as such.

The body follows an internal clock that expects light, meals and activity at roughly the same hours each day. When those hours move, the clock has to reset, and the reset is not instant. A single late night can shift it by an hour or more, and it may take two or three days of regular hours to bring it back. During that time, people often report poor concentration in the morning and hunger at strange times, because the hormones that control appetite follow the same clock.

The practical advice is dull but effective. Choose a waking time you can keep seven days a week, and let your bedtime adjust around it. Get daylight within an hour of waking, ideally by going outside rather than sitting by a window. And keep the last hour before bed free of bright screens, not because the light is harmful in itself, but because it keeps the mind in the state it was in during the day.
第22-25题: Shared bicycles appeared on the Northfield campus two years ago, and in the first month they were treated as a novelty. Students rode them to the station, left them wherever the ride ended, and by the end of the week bicycles were lying across doorways and blocking the ramps used by wheelchair users. The university then introduced a set of rules, and those rules are worth knowing before you unlock your first bicycle.

First, bicycles must be parked in one of the marked areas, which are painted white and can be found outside every teaching building and hall of residence. Leaving a bicycle outside a marked area carries a small charge, and repeated offences lead to the account being suspended for a month. Second, the bicycles are for campus use only. Riding one through the main gate and into the city is not allowed, though many students admit they have done it. Third, riders must be over sixteen, and helmets are strongly recommended but not required.

The most common complaint is not about parking but about maintenance. A bicycle with a broken brake should be reported through the app immediately, and the ride is then free. The company says it repairs reported bicycles within two working days. Last year, it says, the number of accidents on campus fell by a third after the rules came in, which is a result worth remembering the next time you are tempted to leave a bicycle in a doorway.
